title.en: The Mantis's Son, the Baboons, and the Child's Eye
title.zh: 螳螂之子、狒狒與孩童之眼

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), '||Gaunu-tsaxau (the son of the Mantis), the Baboons, and the Mantis'

summary.en: |Kaggen sends his son ||Gaunu-tsaxau to fetch sticks for bows; the baboons mock the child's errand, break his skull and play ball with his eye. The Mantis dreams the crime, flies down, snatches the eye into his bag, and drops it into the water — and the boy rises from the pool, weak but alive.
summary.zh: 卡根遣子取木，狒狒譏其使命，碎其顱，以眼作球戲之。卡根夢知其事，飛下奪眼入囊，投之於水——孩童自池中復起，體弱而生。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings, not as permission to speak for living San communities.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore, ||Gaunu-tsaxau (the son of the Mantis), the Baboons, and the Mantis (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim. ||Gaunu-tsaxau went to fetch sticks for his father, so that the Mantis might take aim at the people who sit upon their heels. An old baboon questioned him, and as the errand was passed from baboon to baboon with their chant 'First going I listen, to the child yonder,' the last of them cried that it was themselves the child was mocking. 'Ye shall strike the child with your fists.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. They struck the child with their fists, breaking his head; another struck out his eye, and the eye rolled away. 'My ball! my ball!' they sang, and played at ball with the child's eye while the child lay still and died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Mantis lay dreaming that the baboons had killed his son and made a ball of his eye. He shut his tears in, slung his rattling quiver, ran to the game, caught the flying eye as it passed, and whirled it round. He threw the eye toward the baboons; it ascended, played in the sky, and sprang into the little bag tied beside his quiver.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He put the child's eye into the water, saying: 'Thou must grow out, that thou mayest become like that which thou hast been.' The child grew again like its former self; the Mantis caught him as he basked by the water, anointed him with his scent, clothed him with the front kaross, and brought him home — while the young Ichneumon cried that the Mantis must have gone to put the eye into the water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—5.; not verbatim.

title.en: The Leopard Tortoise Traps the Hunters' Hands

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡爾維尼亞北方卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Story of the Leopard Tortoise'

summary.en: A sick woman of the early race asks passing hunters to rub her neck with fat; each man's hands decay to bare bone inside her neck. The leopard tortoise always seems about to die — she is the deceiver of the early race.
summary.zh: 早期之民病婦請過路獵者以脂膏擦頸；其手入頸即腐為枯骨。豹龜看似將死——實為早期之民的欺詐者。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The people had gone hunting; she was ill; and she perceived a man who came up to her hut; he had been hunting around. She asked the man to rub her neck a little with fat for her; for, it ached. The man rubbed it with fat for her. And she altogether held the man firmly with it. The man's hands altogether decayed away in it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section I.—7.B, p. 37 (public domain).

passages.text: Again, she espied another man, who came hunting. And she also spoke, she said: 'Rub me with fat a little.' He sat, putting his hands behind him, when the other man came, taking them out from the Leopard Tortoise's neck. He showed the other one his hands; and the other one's hands were altogether inside the Leopard Tortoise's neck.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 37-39; not verbatim.

passages.text: He dashed the Leopard Tortoise upon the ground, while he desired that he should, by dashing it upon the ground, break the Leopard Tortoise. And the Leopard Tortoise held him fast. Then he returned home; and the people said: 'Art thou a fool? Did not thy parents instruct thee? The Leopard Tortoise always seems as if she would die; while she is deceiving us.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 39-41; not verbatim.

title.en: The Moon's Water: Why Game Must Not Be Looked At
title.zh: 月之水：不可注視獵物之故

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Moon is not to be looked at when Game has been shot'

summary.en: After shooting game the hunters may not look at the Moon: the beasts of prey will eat the dying animal. For the Moon's water — the honey-like dew — falls on game and makes it rise again; whoever looks at the Moon lets the game 'go along like the Moon,' away to a waterless place.
summary.zh: 射獲後不得仰月：獸將啖其獵物。月之水如蜜露，落於獸身使其復起；觀月者令獵物如月而行，引至無水之地。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: We may not look at the Moon, when we have shot game; for, we look, lowering our head, while we do not look up, towards the sky; while we are afraid of the Moon's shining. It is that which we fear. For, our mothers used to tell us about it, that the Moon is not a good person, if we look at him. For, if we look at him, when we have shot game, the beasts of prey will eat the game, when the game lies dying, if we look at the Moon.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), section II.—24, p. 67 (public domain).

passages.text: When the game does not die, the Moon's water is that which causes the game to live. For, our mothers used to tell us about it, that, the Moon's water yonder, (that) we see, which is on a bush, it resembles liquid honey. It is that which falls upon the game; the game arises, when it has fallen upon the game. It makes cool the poison with which we shot the game; and the game arises, it goes on... The Moon's water is that which cures it. And it lives, on account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 67-68 (public domain); minor elisions.

passages.text: Therefore, our mothers did not wish us to be looking about, we should not look at the things which are in the sky... that the game which we had shot, would also go along like the Moon... he was not in the habit of going to a place near at hand, for, the day was used to break, while he was still going along. The game would also do the same, if we had looked at the Moon... we could go to die of thirst, while it, leading us astray, took us away to a place where no water was.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 68-69; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mantis Throws His Shoe into the Sky: Origin of the Moon
title.zh: 螳螂擲鞋上天：月亮之源起

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§ 3 and 16; Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), footnote to p. 53

summary.en: Piercing the eland's gall, the Mantis creates a darkness into which he springs. Grope-blind among the bushes, he snatches off his shoe — dust and all — and throws it into the sky: 'this my shoe shall verily become the Moon, which shines in the dark.' The Moon is cold because it is leather; it is red because of the dust of Bushmanland; and it dies and lives again like a shoe thrown up and falling away.
summary.zh: 螳螂刺破羚膽，造暗而躍入。摸索林中，急脫其鞋連塵擲天：「吾鞋必為月，暗中照耀。」月冷因皮革；月紅因桑人之塵；月死而復生，如鞋拋落復揚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition from ||kabbo and Dia!kwain lines of the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: His thinking-strings quickly told him to take off his shoe and throw it up into the sky, for the shoe to light up the earth for him. So he quickly snatched off the shoe from his foot, with the dust on it, he quickly threw it up... Then he saw the Mierkats standing cutting up the Eland in the dark.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), 'The Mantis makes an Eland' (public domain).

passages.text: The Mantis said to them: 'You must hold a torch to light yourselves in cutting up the Eland, but my shoe stands up there in the sky where I have thrown it, to shine for me...' He said: 'I am the Mantis, and this my shoe shall verily become the moon which shines in the dark.' That is why the moon shines at night. That is why the moon is cold, because it is a shoe, it is leather. It is red, because it has earth on it, the dust in which the Mantis had walked.
passages.note: Quote from D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924) (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the long version: he threw the feather up, he said: 'Thou must now lie up in the sky, thou must henceforth be the Moon. Thou shalt shine at night. Thou shalt by thy shining lighten the darkness for men, till the Sun rises to light up all things for men... Thou art the Moon, thou dost give light for men, then thou dost fall away, thou dost return to life, when thou hast fallen away.' That is what the Moon does.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends (1924), pp. 9-10; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun's Knife Cuts the Moon Away

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1875 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §§ 15-16; Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), pp. 50-53

summary.en: In astrological Bushman mythology the Moon is a man whom the Sun, jealous of his night light, stabs and cuts away with his knife of rays until one small piece is left — which the Moon piteously begs the Sun to spare for his children. From that backbone the Moon grows whole again, and the cutting begins again.
summary.zh: 桑人星象神話中，月本為人，因夜光遭日妒，被日以光芒之刀節節割削，僅餘小塊——月哀求日為其孩童留此脊椎。自小塊復長圓盈，割削復始。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition from the Bleek & Lloyd archive; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Sun comes, the Sun follows the darkness, the Sun takes away the moon, the moon stands, the Sun pierces it, with the Sun's knife, as it stands; therefore, it decays away on account of it. Therefore, it says: 'O Sun! leave for the children the backbone!' Therefore, the Sun leaves the backbone for the children; the Sun does so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 51 (public domain).

passages.text: The Moon meant mankind to be like himself: dying, and then coming again living back... he again goes to become another moon, which is whole; he again lives... while he feels that he had seemed to die. Therefore, he becomes a new moon; while he feels that he has again put on a stomach; he becomes large; he comes, while he is alive. He goes along at night... while he feels that he is a shoe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 52-53 (public domain), in the Sun-and-children narration.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of W. H. I. Bleek's 1875 summary (§16): the Moon is looked upon as a man who incurs the wrath of the Sun, and is consequently pierced by the knife (rays) of the latter, until almost the whole of the Moon is cut away, and only one little piece left; which the Moon piteously implores the Sun to spare for his children. From this little piece the Moon gradually grows again until it becomes a full moon, when the Sun's stabbing recommences.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §16; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl of the Early Race Who Made Stars

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871-1873 by ||kabbo (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Girl of the Early Race, who made Stars'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §23

summary.en: In her seclusion hut a girl of the ancient race, angry that her mother gives her too few |hum roots, throws wood-ashes into the sky — they become the Milky Way — and the roots become the red and white stars, while the peel of her food becomes locusts. She was at last shot by her husband. This is the star-creation story of the |Xam.
summary.zh: 初潮隔離之少女，怨母予根少，擲灰上天成銀河；根化紅白之星；果皮化飛蝗。後為夫所射。此即|Xam造星之神話。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd; girlhood seclusion customs are described; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

narrative.en:
The girl of the early race had reached the age when a Bushman girl is put into a tiny hut with a very small door, which her mother closes upon her. She must not look at the springbok, lest they grow wild; she must not look afar. Her mother brings her food. One day the mother gave her too little of the |hum, the scented root eaten raw, and the girl grew hungry and angry in her hut.

She took up wood-ashes and threw them into the sky, saying: 'The wood ashes which are here, they must altogether become the Milky Way; they must white lie along in the sky, that the stars may stand outside of the Milky Way.' The ashes became the glowing arch of the night, and the stars, she said, should sail along their footprints, standing brightly around, so that the people might find their way home by night, in the middle of the night.

Still angry, she threw up the roots of the |hum she had been given: the red old roots became the red stars and the white young roots the white stars. Then she threw up the peel of the |khissi root she was eating, and the peel became locusts. The Milky Way gently glows, it is said, because it feels that it is wood ashes; it lights a little, so that the people can return home.

But the myth closes darkly. The first girl of the early race acted ill, the narrators say; and she was at last shot by her husband. Girls who transgressed the seclusion rules could fix with their glance the people and things they looked at (§24 of Bleek's Brief Account records men turned into trees by a maiden's glance), and the star-maker's fate warns against the powers of the isolated girl. Her creation stands: every clear night the ashes still lie white along the sky, and the stars sail along behind them. The narrators add the frame: the \xwi-\na-ssho-\k'e, the people of the early race, were said to be stupid and not to have understood things well; their doings are retold so that the Flat Bushmen may know what the first inhabitants of the land did. The girl's ashes were the first light of the night road, and her angry root-throwing peopled the sky; the Milky Way must go round with the stars, lying as it goes, and when the sun turns back the stars also turn back to fetch the daybreak. Bushman children are shown the arch and told that it gently glows because it remembers being wood ashes; and mothers warn their daughters in the seclusion hut with the same story, so that the angry, hungry girl inside the little door is also the maker of the stars she may not stare at too long.

functions: Charter narrative for the Milky Way and the stars of the |Xam sky.
Teaches the girlhood seclusion rules: what a maiden must not eat, see, or do.
Links anger and hunger in the seclusion hut to cosmic creation.

variants.name: Katkop-dialect girl (Dia!kwain's mother's telling)
variants.summary: A variant on the same seclusion girl exists in the Katkop dialect told to Dia!kwain by his mother, with the root-throwing episode elaborated.

variants.name: Maiden who fixed people as trees (Bleek §38)
variants.summary: Another maiden's glance turned people into talking trees; related to the same seclusion powers.

primary_sources.citation: London: George Allen & Co., 1911, pp. 72-77; manuscript L II.—28. 2505-2520

primary_sources.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts

secondary_sources.work: D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends
secondary_sources.citation: Bleek, D. F. 1924. London: George Allen & Unwin.

secondary_sources.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing: Symbolic Meanings in Southern San Rock Paintings
secondary_sources.citation: Lewis-Williams, J. D. 1981. London: Academic Press.

source_urls.description: Scanned copy of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911)
Bleek's Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (1875)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Collected under colonial constraint (some informants were prisoners at the Breakwater); girls' rites appear here through male-colonial transcription — present with archival framing only.

passages.text: My mother was the one who told me that the girl arose; she put her hands into the wood ashes; she threw up the wood ashes into the sky. She said to the wood ashes: 'The wood ashes which are here, they must altogether become the Milky Way. They must white lie along in the sky, that the stars may stand outside of the Milky Way, while the Milky Way is the Milky Way, while it used to be wood ashes.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 73 (public domain).

passages.text: The Milky Way lying comes to its place... that it may descend nicely... The Stars shall also stand nicely around. They shall sail along upon their footprints, which they, always sailing along, are following... The Stars had been setting; they had, again, been coming out; they had, sailing along, been following their footprints. They become white, when the Sun comes out.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 75 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She first gently threw up wood ashes into the sky, that she might presently throw up |hum roots; while she felt that she was angry with her mother, because her mother had not given her many |hum roots, that she might eat abundantly; for, she was in the hut. The red roots made red stars and the white roots white stars; the peel of the |khissi root she threw up became locusts. And the girl was at last shot by her husband.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 76-77; not verbatim.

title.en: \gaunu, the Great Star Who Named the Stars
title.zh: 大星加烏奴：命名眾星者

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Great Star, \gaunu, which, singing, named the Stars'

summary.en: \gaunu was once a great star; singing, he called out the names of all the stars, which is why the stars possess their names. The smallest, fine stars he made '\whai' — identified by the observatory with Altair and its neighbours — and the porcupine watches for them, for when they turn back it is dawn and he goes home.
summary.zh: 加烏奴昔為大星，唱而呼眾星之名，故眾星有其名。至小至細者，其名為'瓦海——經天文臺證為牛郎星（天鷹座α）。穿山甲候之：星回則天明，遂歸家。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; star identifications by Royal Observatory astronomers, 1873.

passages.text: \gaunu, he was formerly a great Star; therefore, his name is \gaunu, while he feels that he was the one who formerly spoke (called) the Stars' names; while he feels that he is a great one. Therefore, he called the Stars' names. Therefore, the Stars possess their names; while they feel that \gaunu was the one who called their names.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 79 (public domain).

passages.text: He formerly sang, while he uttered the Stars' names. He said '\whai' to (some) Stars which are very small; they are those of which he made '\whai'; their small, fine ones are those which are '\whai'. [The stars \whai-gwai and \whai-|pua were identified as Altair and neighbouring stars of Aquila.]
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 79 with editor's bracketed note (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore, the porcupine, when these Stars have, sitting, turned back, he will not remain on the hunting ground; for, he knows that it is dawn, when '\whai' has, lying, turned back. He returns home; for, he is used to look at these Stars; they are those which he watches.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 81 (public domain).

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'What the Stars say, and a Prayer to a Star'

summary.en: On summer nights the stars cry 'Tsau! Tsau!' — they are cursing the shining eyes of springbok and the beasts of prey, which also gleam in the dark. The Bushman listens to the stars as a boy sleeping beside his grandfather, and learns their speech.
summary.zh: 夏夜星辰呼「呲！呲！」——詛咒羚羊與猛獸暗中閃耀之目。桑人童子偎祖父而眠，聆聽星語。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: They (the Bushmen) wish, that they may also perceive things. Therefore, they say that the Star shall take their heart, with which they do not a little hunger; the Star shall give them the Star's heart, — the Star's heart, — with which the Star sits in plenty. For the Star is not small; the Star seems as if it had food.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 81 (public domain).

passages.text: The Stars are wont to call, 'Tsau! Tsau!' therefore the Bushmen are wont to say, that the Stars curse for them the springboks' eyes; the Stars say, 'Tsau!' they say, 'Tsau! Tsau!' I am one who was listening to them. I questioned my grandfather, what things it could be that spoke thus. My grandfather said to me that the Stars were those who spoke thus.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 81-82 (public domain).

passages.text: The Stars said, 'Tsau! Tsau!' Summer is (the time) when they sound. Because I used to sleep with my grandfather, I was the one who sat with my grandfather, when he sat in the coolness outside. Therefore, I questioned him, about the things which spoke thus. He said, the Stars were those who spoke thus; they cursed for the people the springboks' eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 82-83 (public domain).

title.en: The Prayer to Canopus for a Shooting Arm

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'What the Stars say, and a Prayer to a Star'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §60

summary.en: When Canopus rises the old man speaks to the 'Bushman-rice' star: give me thy heart, take mine; give me thy stomach, take mine; give me thy arm, which never misses — for my arm misses its aim. He speaks the prayer sitting in the cool, wishing the arrow might hit the springbok for him.
summary.zh: 老人星升時，老者向「桑人之米」星祈曰：取我之心，予爾飽足之心；取我之臂——常失之臂——予爾百發百中之臂。坐於涼處誦禱，望箭中羚。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My grandfather used to speak to Canopus, when Canopus had newly come out; he said: 'Thou shalt give me thy heart, with which thou dost sit in plenty, thou shalt take my heart, — my heart, — with which I am desperately hungry. That I might also be full, like thee. For, I hunger. For, thou seemest to be satisfied (with food); hence thou art not small. For, I am hungry.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 83 (public domain).

passages.text: 'Thou shalt give me thy stomach, with which thou art satisfied. Thou shalt take my stomach, that thou mayst also hunger. Give thou me also thy arm, thou shalt take my arm, with which I do not kill. For, I miss my aim. Thou shalt give me thy arm. For, my arm which is here, I miss my aim with it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 83 (public domain).

passages.text: He desired that the arrow might hit the springbok for him; hence, he wished the Star to give him the Star's arm, while the Star took his arm, with which he missed his aim. He shut his mouth, he moved away, he sat down; while he felt that he wished to sit and sharpen an arrow.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 83-84 (public domain).
